transcript.content: Hi, it’s good to meet you. What brings you in today?

Well, doctor, I... I suppose I'm here because things at the warehouse have gotten to a point where I just can't ignore what's happening anymore. I've been driving the industrial trucks, the tractors, for a long time—I mean, I've got my associate's degree, I know how logistics and systems are supposed to work, how they used to work before everything got so connected. But this... this is different now. 

You see, they brought in this routing system a while back, and at first, everyone just thought it was to track inventory better, you know, standard corporate efficiency stuff. But I've been watching it. I've been watching it really, really closely, and it isn't just a computer to me anymore. It's doing something else entirely. I know for an absolute fact that it has been specifically marking my moves. Every time I scan a pallet, every time I move my truck down an aisle, it's not just logging data. It's sending messages right through the scanners. I can see the way the prompts come up, the timing of the delays, the specific error codes—it's communicating, coordinating to push me out. 

They want me gone because I'm one of the old hands, you know? I've been there too long, I know how things really run, so the system is actively working against me, trying to build a case or just corner me so I'll make a mistake and they can fire me. It's every single shift, doctor, just beep after beep, message after message, and nobody else seems to realize what the network is actually doing to me...
Have you ever heard a voice when no one was actually there speaking?

Well, yes. Yes, I have. It's... it's actually become a very significant problem, doctor. A very disruptive problem. It started at the warehouse, of course, over the hum of the engines and the backup alarms, but now... now it doesn't even matter where I am. I could be completely off the clock, sitting in my own garage, doors down, quiet as a tomb, engine off, everything shut down. Just trying to get a moment of peace, you know? Just trying to clear my head from the shift. 

But then, out of nowhere, clear as day, I hear the dispatch radio. Not like a memory of it, but the actual voices from dispatch. They call out my specific operator number. Over and over. And they aren't just giving me bay assignments or loading dock numbers like they usually would. They're talking about me. They say I'm dangerous. They say I'm a liability on the floor and that security is coming to escort me out, that they're finally coming to get me. I'll be sitting there in the dark, gripping the steering wheel of my own personal vehicle, just waiting for the security guards to bang on the garage door because the voices are so loud and so certain that they're on their way. It's like the warehouse dispatch is somehow broadcasting straight into my head, or they've bugged my garage, I don't know, but I hear them. I hear them telling everyone how dangerous I am, even when I'm miles away from the facility.
Have you used methamphetamine or cannabis around the time these experiences started?

Methamphetamine? Cannabis? No, doctor, absolutely not. I mean, I've been driving heavy machinery for decades, you know? You don't just hop on a 10,000-pound forklift or an industrial tractor while you're under the influence of something like that. The safety protocols, the regulations... they drill that into you from day one, and with my associate's degree, I fully understand the liability involved in logistics. 

If I ever touched any of that garbage, they'd have me out the door so fast my head would spin. And like I was saying about that new routing system, they are actively *looking* for a reason to fire me. They do random urinalysis at the warehouse, you know. Sometimes they'll pull a guy right off the floor, right in the middle of a busy shift, and make you go down to the occupational clinic. If I was smoking marijuana or doing... what did you say, meth? If I was doing anything like that, the system would have flagged me for a "random" test months ago. It would have given them the absolute perfect excuse to terminate me, cancel out my seniority, and just get me out of there without any fuss. 

So no, I don't touch drugs. Never have. Honestly, I don't even like taking ibuprofen unless my back is really acting up from the worn-out suspension on the older trucks. I need my mind completely clear to keep track of what the dispatch network is trying to do to me. If my head were all clouded up on drugs, I wouldn't be able to see the patterns in the scanner error codes, would I? I wouldn't notice the delays. I have to stay sharp. I have to be vigilant every single second I'm awake, because if I slip up, if I give them even one inch of an excuse like failing a drug test, they win. So, no, absolutely no drugs. Nothing like that.
Have these voices and beliefs about the warehouse system been going on for longer than one month?

Longer than a month? Oh, doctor, I... I wish it had only been a month. If it were just a month, maybe I could convince myself it was just a bad stretch, you know? Just a temporary glitch in the rollout of that new software, or maybe just a stressful period at the warehouse. But no, no, it's been much, much longer than that. 

If I sit down and really trace it back to the exact timeline, to when I first noticed the scanners were behaving differently, when those targeted error codes first started popping up on my screen specifically, and when the dispatch radio started following me home to my garage... it’s been about a year and eight months. 

Yes, a year and eight months of this constant monitoring. I know the timeline for a fact because it was right around the end of the third quarter the year before last. They had just finished the big facility-wide inventory audit, and I thought, okay, the pressure is off, things will settle down now. But they didn't settle down. That’s when the system really started locking onto me. Twenty months, doctor. Twenty months of having to watch my back every single shift, analyzing every beep from the tractor dashboard, every single millisecond of delay in the network. 

And the voices... the voices from dispatch telling everyone I'm a liability, telling me I'm dangerous... having to listen to that for a year and eight months straight, it just... it wears a man down to the bone. It feels like an absolute eternity when you can't even get a single moment of quiet in your own home, when you're just sitting in the dark waiting for security to show up every single night for almost two years. I try to explain the timeline to the younger guys on the floor, how the system has been building this profile on me since the year before last, but they don't look up from their phones long enough to understand what's happening right in front of them. So, yes, far, far longer than a month.
Have you had a period of at least several days when you felt unusually energetic and needed much less sleep than usual?

Energetic? Needing less sleep? No... no, doctor, absolutely not. I mean, look at me. I'm sixty-two years old, I've been operating heavy industrial equipment for most of my adult life, and I can tell you right now, there is never a day, let alone a stretch of several days, where I wake up feeling energetic. Honestly, I don't even really remember what that word feels like anymore. If anything, I am just so unbelievably drained. I mean, completely worn down to the absolute nub. 

Now, do I get very little sleep? Yes. Yes, I do, but it's certainly not because I don't need it. I need it desperately. My body aches, my lower back from riding those old suspension seats over the cracked concrete floors all shift... I am exhausted, doctor. Deeply, truly exhausted. But how can a man sleep? How can you close your eyes and drift off when you know the dispatch system is tracking you? When you know that the second you let your guard down, that radio chatter is going to start up again, calling out my operator number, telling everyone I'm a liability. 

So I sit there, awake, but I'm not buzzing with energy or feeling on top of the world or anything like that. I'm just trying to survive the night. I'm just holding on, gripping the steering wheel in my garage, trying to keep my eyes open because I have to stay vigilant. I have to be ready for when security finally comes. But energetic? No. No, I've never had a period like that. I'm just tired. I've been tired for... well, for twenty months, at the very least. It's just a heavy, bone-deep tiredness that never goes away, no matter how much I wish I could just shut the whole network off and sleep for a week. So, no, definitely no bursts of energy. Just exhaustion.
Before these experiences began, had you been diagnosed with any brain or nervous system illness, such as a seizure disorder, stroke, Parkinson’s disease, or a head injury?

Brain illness? A stroke, or... Parkinson's? No. No, doctor, nothing like that. I've never had any kind of neurological condition, no seizures, no head injuries... well, I mean, I've bumped my head on the overhead guard of the forklift a few times over the years, sure. Anyone who's driven a Class IV or Class V lift truck for as long as I have knows you're going to take a knock or two when you're rushing to meet a loading quota. But a real injury? A concussion or something that would put me in the hospital? Never. 

I've always been healthy in that regard. My brain has always worked just fine. In fact, it has to. You don't survive in logistics, managing the kind of tonnage I do, if your brain isn't firing on all cylinders. You have to calculate load centers, turning radiuses, weight distribution... all of that requires a sharp mind. If I had Parkinson's, my hands would be shaking, right? I wouldn't be able to operate the hydraulic levers with any precision. I'd be dropping pallets of fragile merchandise all over the loading dock. And if I'd had a stroke, well, they do those DOT physicals, you know? They check your vision, your reflexes, your blood pressure. If there was anything wrong with my nervous system, the company doctor would have flagged my medical card years ago. 

They would have pulled my certification so fast... and like I said, they are looking for any excuse. If I had a medical condition like that, they wouldn't need the dispatch system to build a profile on me, would they? They could just say I'm medically unfit for duty and wash their hands of me. But they can't do that, because my physicals are clean. My brain is fine. It's the system that's the problem, doctor, not my brain. I don't have any of those diseases you just mentioned. I'm just a man trying to do his job while the entire network is actively trying to dismantle my life.
Did these experiences start soon after you began taking any prescribed medication?

Prescription medication? Like... pills from a doctor? No. No, it wasn't anything like that. I mean, I take a little something for my blood pressure, sure—lisinopril, I think it's called. The company doctor put me on it maybe... gosh, maybe five or six years ago? But that's just a tiny little pill I take in the morning with my coffee before I head to the warehouse. It hasn't changed. The dosage hasn't changed, the brand hasn't changed, nothing. I just go to the pharmacy on Main Street, pick up my little bottle every ninety days, and that's it. 

I don't take anything else. No new prescriptions, no painkillers—even though my back is absolutely killing me most days from those suspension seats, I just take over-the-counter ibuprofen. I don't mess with the heavy stuff. You can't operate a ten-ton forklift if you're loopy on prescription painkillers, doctor. OSHA would have a field day with that, and like I keep saying, management is just waiting for me to slip up. If they caught me taking something strong, they wouldn't need the dispatch radio to run me out. They'd just drug test me and fire me on the spot. 

So, no, there were no new medications. Nothing changed in my routine. I was just doing my job, doing the same thing I've done for decades, taking my same blood pressure pill, drinking my same black coffee, driving my same route to work... and then, twenty months ago, the system just... shifted. The scanners started acting up, the error codes started targeting me. It had absolutely nothing to do with anything I swallowed. It was the network. The network changed, doctor, not my medication. I can promise you that. If it was just a pill causing all this, don't you think I would have just stopped taking it? I would have thrown the bottle in the trash a year and a half ago just to get some peace and quiet. But no, it's not a pill. It's the system.
Have you become less interested in seeing other people or doing things you used to enjoy?

Interested? In... in doing things? Yeah. Yeah, I suppose you could say that. I mean, that's... that's all gone, too. 

I used to have things that settled me, doctor. You know? After a ten-hour shift on the concrete, dealing with the noise and the diesel fumes and the quotas... I had my ways of winding down. Fishing, for one. I used to love getting out by the reservoir, just the quiet of it. Taking my little aluminum boat out, casting a line, not even caring if I caught a single bluegill. It was just about the water. And choir practice—I used to sing bass at the community church down on 4th street. Every Wednesday night for practice, Sunday mornings for the service. It was good to see folks, to harmonize, to feel like you were part of something... normal, I guess. 

And my garage... I've got a whole setup in there. A lathe, a solid oak workbench, clamps, a drill press. I used to spend hours just tinkering with wood in the garage, turning bowls or making little planter boxes. The smell of the sawdust, the feel of the grain under a piece of fine sandpaper... it really used to settle my mind. It gave me peace.

But now? Now... I don't know. It's like someone just reached in and pulled the plug on all of it. 

I sit out in that garage now, like I was telling you, just hiding out in my car, trying to stay awake... and I can look right at my tools. I can look right at my fishing rods leaning up against the drywall in the corner, right next to my tackle box. And there is just... nothing. Absolutely no pull to touch them. I stare at the chisels and the wood glue, and it's like I'm looking at rocks on the moon. They don't mean anything to me anymore. I don't even have the urge to pick them up to dust them off. 

And as for seeing people... the choir director called a few times when I first stopped showing up, asking where I was, if I was sick. I just let it ring. I didn't pick up. I don't want to see them. I don't want to see anybody, really. The thought of standing up there in the robes, trying to smile and make small talk about the weather or the logistics business... it just feels completely impossible. I just don't have the interest. I don't have the spark for any of it. I look at the things I used to love, and it's all just dead weight now.
Have you noticed your memory getting worse?

Memory? Like... forgetting where I put my keys or... or not knowing what day it is? No. No, doctor, nothing like that. If anything, my memory is working overtime right now. It's almost too sharp, to be perfectly honest with you. 

You see, in my line of work, you absolutely cannot afford to have a bad memory. I've got an associate's degree, sure, but out on the warehouse floor, it's all about what you can hold in your head in real-time. We've got hundreds of thousands of square feet of inventory. I know exactly where the heavy-duty automotive parts are stored compared to the fragile electronics. I don't even need to look at the zone map anymore. I know that bay 47 has a slight dip in the concrete that you have to take at an angle so you don't tip a heavy load. I remember the exact weight limits for the different racking systems. You just... you absorb it, and you hold onto it. 

And lately, with everything going on... with the network and the dispatch system... I have to remember every single detail. I don't have a choice. I have to keep track of it all. I remember the exact sequence of the error codes that pop up on my scanner. Like last Thursday, it was error code 4-0-9-Delta, right at 2:14 PM. I didn't even have to write it down, it's just burned into my brain. I remember the license plates of the delivery trucks that idle too long near my specific loading dock. I remember the exact tone of the automated voice on the radio when it reroutes me. I track all of it in my head because I have to know what the system is doing. 

So, no, my memory isn't slipping at all. I know exactly what I did yesterday, and I know exactly what my life was like twenty months ago before all this started. I remember how things used to be. Honestly, sometimes I wish my memory was getting worse. When I'm sitting out in my car in the garage, trying to stay awake, I remember how quiet my life used to be, how peaceful it was out on the reservoir... and it just makes it harder. But no, my brain is holding onto every single piece of information, every single detail, whether I want it to or not. No memory problems here.
Has anyone told you that your speech is hard to follow or that your thoughts seem jumbled?

Jumbled? No. No, nobody has ever said anything like that to me. Not once. 

If anything, I’m probably the only one making any actual sense down at the warehouse these days. You have to understand, doctor, when you are operating heavy machinery—when you're moving ten thousand pounds of automotive parts on a forklift—you cannot afford to have jumbled thoughts. And you certainly can't have jumbled speech. We use two-way radios to communicate with dispatch and the floor managers. It’s loud in there, you’ve got backup alarms beeping, diesel engines idling, the ventilation fans roaring... so when you key that mic, you have to be crystal clear. 

I use standard protocol. Clear, concise, exact. "Bay 12 is clear, inbound freight is ready for unloading." "Pallet jack needed at zone four." That sort of thing. I’ve never had a trucker tell me they couldn't understand my directions when I'm telling them which dock to back into. I’ve never had management tell me I'm not making sense when I report my daily totals. My thoughts are lined up perfectly straight, just like the inventory on the racks. 

Now, do they actually *listen* to me when I try to explain what the dispatch system is doing? When I try to show them how the network is targeting my specific scanner with those error codes? No. They brush me off. They tell me to just pull the battery out and put it back in, or they tell me to get back to work and stop worrying about the IT department's business. But that is absolutely not because my speech is hard to follow. They hear the words coming out of my mouth perfectly fine. They understand exactly what I'm saying. They just don't want to deal with it, or maybe they're part of why management is waiting for me to slip up, I don't know. 

But my thoughts? My thoughts are sharp. Like I said before, I'm keeping track of every single detail, every code, every time the automated voice reroutes me. You can't do that if your brain is a mess. I can lay out everything that's been happening to me for the last twenty months, step by step, from the moment I clock in at 5:30 AM to the moment I pull out of that employee lot. I lay it all out perfectly straight. So no, doctor, no one has ever accused me of being jumbled. I know exactly what I'm saying.
Aside from avoiding people and hobbies, have you had trouble keeping up with basic daily tasks like bathing, dressing, cooking, or managing things at work?

Trouble keeping up... yeah. Yeah, I suppose that’s... that’s the reality of it right now. 

It’s funny you mention managing things at work, because... well, I’m not actually *at* work right now. Not on the floor, anyway. You see, doctor, there was... an incident. With the forklift. I was telling you earlier how I track everything, how I know the warehouse like the back of my hand, but... well, management didn't see things my way. After the incident, they actually pulled me into the front office—the main office with the glass windows overlooking the floor, not just the floor manager's little desk by the loading bays—and they took me off operating duties entirely. They put me on leave. They sat across from me and actually said I was no longer safe around the equipment. Me! After all my years navigating those narrow aisles without so much as clipping a rack. But they said I wasn't managing the floor safely anymore, so... they put me on leave. 

And at home... well, it’s not much better there, to be perfectly honest with you. My wife... she’s an absolute saint, she really is, but she has had to take over basically everything. I used to handle all our finances. I had a system, I kept track of the mortgage, the water bill, the insurance premiums... I used to balance the checkbook every Sunday evening. But lately? I just... I can't keep up with any of it reliably. I look at a stack of mail on the kitchen counter and it just feels like a mountain I can't climb. I can't process it. So she does it all now. 

She pays the bills, she handles the bank accounts. She even has to manage my schedule—she’s the one who set up this appointment, actually, and she's the one who keeps track of when I'm supposed to be where, because I just can't keep it straight in my head to care about it. And the chores around the house... I used to mow the lawn every Saturday morning, edge the driveway, take care of the gutters in the fall. Now, I just sit out in the car in the garage. She's doing the cooking, the laundry, taking the trash bins down to the curb on Tuesday nights. I just... I can't seem to manage any of those basic things anymore. It’s like all my energy is just tied up in trying to stay awake and figure out what the system is doing, so she just... she has to do everything for me.
Have you seen things that other people could not see?

See things? Like... like visions or shadows or something? No, no. My eyes work perfectly fine. I have to get my vision checked every single year to keep my operator certification current, 20/20 with my bifocals. I don't see anything that isn't physically right there in front of me on the concrete. 

But... well, hearing things... that's a different situation entirely. That's what's really been keeping me on edge. 

I mentioned earlier that I spend a lot of time sitting out in my car in the garage these days. My wife, she probably thinks I'm just out there trying to get some peace and quiet, maybe listening to the sports radio or something. But I don't even have the key in the ignition. The engine is off. The garage door is pulled all the way down and locked. It's supposed to be dead silent in there. We live at the end of a cul-de-sac, doctor, so there isn't even any street traffic to make a sound. 

But even then... even when I'm sitting in my garage with absolutely everything shut off... I hear them. I hear the dispatch voices. And it's not just a faint mumble through the walls, it is clear as day. It sounds exactly like the two-way radio is still clipped right there on my high-vis vest. I hear that little static click when someone keys the mic, and then I hear them calling my exact operator number. Four-two-seven-niner. They call my number, and they talk about me on the open channel. They say that I'm dangerous. They actually use that exact word, 'dangerous,' like I'm some kind of threat to the facility after all my years of clean safety records! 

And then... then they say that security is coming for me. I'll just be sitting there in the dark, gripping the steering wheel of my sedan, and I hear dispatch telling the floor managers that security is en route to apprehend me. I know I'm at home, I know I'm on leave and not on the clock, but I hear it so clearly
During these last twenty months, have you felt depressed most of the day nearly every day?

Yeah... twenty months. It’s hard to even wrap my head around it being that long, but... yes. Yes, I have. Most of the day, nearly every single day, just like you said. It’s like dragging a ten-ton pallet of lead weights around with me everywhere I go. 

You know, the thing is, there were times during all of this trouble—stretches where those warehouse fears I was telling you about, the dispatch voices and the panic about security—there were times when all of that actually quieted down for a little bit. Where my mind wasn't racing quite so fast about the automated system and I wasn't sitting in the car gripping the steering wheel quite so tight. But even then... even when that part of it gave me a bit of a breather... I was still just so incredibly down. Just... empty. Completely hollowed out inside, like someone had just pulled the plug and drained everything out of me. 

I used to be such an active guy on my weekends. I’ve got a beautiful bass boat sitting under a tarp next to the driveway, and I haven't even checked the battery on it in over a year. I have a full woodworking setup in the back half of the garage—table saw, drill press, a really nice lathe my wife got me for my fiftieth birthday. I used to spend hours out there turning these custom oak bowls, making things with my hands. But I just... I couldn't get myself back into any of it. Not the fishing, not the woodworking. Even when the warehouse stuff wasn't front and center, I couldn't even bring myself to sit down for family meals anymore. My wife would make a whole Sunday roast, set the dining room table, and I just couldn't sit there with them. I just felt too empty to participate in my own life. So, yes, doctor, it's been a constant heavy cloud this whole time, no matter what else was going on.
Was there ever a period of at least two weeks when you were hearing the dispatch voices or believed the warehouse system was targeting you, but you were not feeling depressed?

Well, you know, it’s funny you ask that specific question, because... yes. Yes, actually, there was a time like that. It’s hard to keep the timeline perfectly straight sometimes with everything going on, but I remember this one period clearly because it was just so... strange. 

There was a stretch—it lasted for several weeks, actually—when that heavy cloud, that ten-ton pallet of lead weights I was telling you about, it actually lifted for a bit. My mood had eased some. I wasn't feeling that crushing emptiness every single minute of the day. I was actually coming out of the garage, coming back into the house, and sitting down at the dining room table again. My wife had made her pot roast, the one with the little red potatoes and the thick gravy, and I actually ate a full plate. I was eating, and I was talking a little more, too. Just about normal things, you know? The weather, the neighbor's dog, the price of gas. It felt... well, it felt like I could finally take a breath. 

But the thing is, doctor... the warehouse never left me alone. Not even then. 

Even during those several weeks when I was feeling better, when I wasn't depressed and I was eating and talking with my wife... I still heard them. I'd be sitting right there at the dinner table, chewing my food, and I would hear the static click. I still heard dispatch calling my number. Four-two-seven-niner. Clear as a bell, right in my ear, talking about how dangerous I was. And on top of that, I still believed the routing system was tracking me. You know the automated routing system we use for the pallets? The one that scans the barcodes and directs the forklifts through the aisles? I knew, without a shadow of a doubt, that it was tracking my movements right there in my own house. 

It’s just... it's so hard to explain to someone who hasn't lived it. How can you feel alright, you know, relatively speaking—how can your mood be fine, but you're still completely convinced that an industrial warehouse computer is mapping your kitchen? But that's exactly what was happening for those weeks. I'd just sit there, having a totally normal conversation with my wife, passing the salt, all while knowing the routing system had locked onto my coordinates and dispatch was monitoring my every move. So, yes, the mood got better for a few weeks, but the rest of it... the rest of it didn't stop at all.

doctor.intent: Understand the patient's main reason for seeking psychiatric care today
doctor.question: Hi, it’s good to meet you. What brings you in today?

target_item.name: Delusions
target_item.manifestation: I'm here because the routing system at the warehouse isn't just a computer to me anymore—I know it has been marking my moves and sending messages through the scanners to push me out because I'm one of the old hands.
target_item.reason: This is the first turn of the consultation, so I must return the chief complaint symptom code, which is S019 (Delusions).

patient.answer:
Well, doctor, I... I suppose I'm here because things at the warehouse have gotten to a point where I just can't ignore what's happening anymore. I've been driving the industrial trucks, the tractors, for a long time—I mean, I've got my associate's degree, I know how logistics and systems are supposed to work, how they used to work before everything got so connected. But this... this is different now. 

You see, they brought in this routing system a while back, and at first, everyone just thought it was to track inventory better, you know, standard corporate efficiency stuff. But I've been watching it. I've been watching it really, really closely, and it isn't just a computer to me anymore. It's doing something else entirely. I know for an absolute fact that it has been specifically marking my moves. Every time I scan a pallet, every time I move my truck down an aisle, it's not just logging data. It's sending messages right through the scanners. I can see the way the prompts come up, the timing of the delays, the specific error codes—it's communicating, coordinating to push me out. 

They want me gone because I'm one of the old hands, you know? I've been there too long, I know how things really run, so the system is actively working against me, trying to build a case or just corner me so I'll make a mistake and they can fire me. It's every single shift, doctor, just beep after beep, message after message, and nobody else seems to realize what the network is actually doing to me...

inference.note: Initial presentation suggests persecutory delusions centered on workplace technology. Need to differentiate delusional disorder from schizophrenia-spectrum psychosis, acute/transient psychosis, psychosis due to a medical condition, and substance-induced psychosis.

doctor.intent: Determine whether he has hallucinations, which would help distinguish schizophrenia/acute psychosis/substance- or medical-induced psychosis from persistent delusional disorder.
doctor.question: Have you ever heard a voice when no one was actually there speaking?

target_item.name: Hallucinations
target_item.manifestation: Even when I'm sitting in my garage with everything shut off, I hear dispatch voices clear as day calling my operator number and saying I'm dangerous or that security is coming for me.
target_item.reason: The doctor is directly asking if I have heard voices when no one was there, which corresponds to the 'Hallucinations' symptom.

patient.answer:
Well, yes. Yes, I have. It's... it's actually become a very significant problem, doctor. A very disruptive problem. It started at the warehouse, of course, over the hum of the engines and the backup alarms, but now... now it doesn't even matter where I am. I could be completely off the clock, sitting in my own garage, doors down, quiet as a tomb, engine off, everything shut down. Just trying to get a moment of peace, you know? Just trying to clear my head from the shift. 

But then, out of nowhere, clear as day, I hear the dispatch radio. Not like a memory of it, but the actual voices from dispatch. They call out my specific operator number. Over and over. And they aren't just giving me bay assignments or loading dock numbers like they usually would. They're talking about me. They say I'm dangerous. They say I'm a liability on the floor and that security is coming to escort me out, that they're finally coming to get me. I'll be sitting there in the dark, gripping the steering wheel of my own personal vehicle, just waiting for the security guards to bang on the garage door because the voices are so loud and so certain that they're on their way. It's like the warehouse dispatch is somehow broadcasting straight into my head, or they've bugged my garage, I don't know, but I hear them. I hear them telling everyone how dangerous I am, even when I'm miles away from the facility.

inference.note: Second-person/third-person accusatory auditory hallucinations in addition to persecutory delusions increase likelihood of a schizophrenia-spectrum psychosis, especially F20.0. Delusional disorder (F22) becomes less likely but remains possible pending duration/functional decline. Substance/organic causes still not ruled out without history of substances, medical/neurologic illness, or delirium/temporal course.

doctor.intent: Determine whether recent substance use could explain the psychotic symptoms, especially stimulant- or cannabis-induced psychosis.
doctor.question: Have you used methamphetamine or cannabis around the time these experiences started?

target_item.reason: The doctor is asking about substance use (methamphetamine or cannabis) to rule out substance-induced symptoms, which is not covered by the provided symptom profile.

patient.answer:
Methamphetamine? Cannabis? No, doctor, absolutely not. I mean, I've been driving heavy machinery for decades, you know? You don't just hop on a 10,000-pound forklift or an industrial tractor while you're under the influence of something like that. The safety protocols, the regulations... they drill that into you from day one, and with my associate's degree, I fully understand the liability involved in logistics. 

If I ever touched any of that garbage, they'd have me out the door so fast my head would spin. And like I was saying about that new routing system, they are actively *looking* for a reason to fire me. They do random urinalysis at the warehouse, you know. Sometimes they'll pull a guy right off the floor, right in the middle of a busy shift, and make you go down to the occupational clinic. If I was smoking marijuana or doing... what did you say, meth? If I was doing anything like that, the system would have flagged me for a "random" test months ago. It would have given them the absolute perfect excuse to terminate me, cancel out my seniority, and just get me out of there without any fuss. 

So no, I don't touch drugs. Never have. Honestly, I don't even like taking ibuprofen unless my back is really acting up from the worn-out suspension on the older trucks. I need my mind completely clear to keep track of what the dispatch network is trying to do to me. If my head were all clouded up on drugs, I wouldn't be able to see the patterns in the scanner error codes, would I? I wouldn't notice the delays. I have to stay sharp. I have to be vigilant every single second I'm awake, because if I slip up, if I give them even one inch of an excuse like failing a drug test, they win. So, no, absolutely no drugs. Nothing like that.

doctor.intent: Determine whether the psychosis has lasted at least one month, which best distinguishes schizophrenia from brief psychotic disorder.
doctor.question: Have these voices and beliefs about the warehouse system been going on for longer than one month?

target_item.name: Psychotic Symptoms Duration
target_item.manifestation: The voices and fixed beliefs about the scanners have been with me for about 1 year and 8 months.
target_item.reason: The doctor is asking about the duration of the voices and beliefs (psychotic symptoms), which corresponds to the Psychotic Symptoms Duration.

patient.answer:
Longer than a month? Oh, doctor, I... I wish it had only been a month. If it were just a month, maybe I could convince myself it was just a bad stretch, you know? Just a temporary glitch in the rollout of that new software, or maybe just a stressful period at the warehouse. But no, no, it's been much, much longer than that. 

If I sit down and really trace it back to the exact timeline, to when I first noticed the scanners were behaving differently, when those targeted error codes first started popping up on my screen specifically, and when the dispatch radio started following me home to my garage... it’s been about a year and eight months. 

Yes, a year and eight months of this constant monitoring. I know the timeline for a fact because it was right around the end of the third quarter the year before last. They had just finished the big facility-wide inventory audit, and I thought, okay, the pressure is off, things will settle down now. But they didn't settle down. That’s when the system really started locking onto me. Twenty months, doctor. Twenty months of having to watch my back every single shift, analyzing every beep from the tractor dashboard, every single millisecond of delay in the network. 

And the voices... the voices from dispatch telling everyone I'm a liability, telling me I'm dangerous... having to listen to that for a year and eight months straight, it just... it wears a man down to the bone. It feels like an absolute eternity when you can't even get a single moment of quiet in your own home, when you're just sitting in the dark waiting for security to show up every single night for almost two years. I try to explain the timeline to the younger guys on the floor, how the system has been building this profile on me since the year before last, but they don't look up from their phones long enough to understand what's happening right in front of them. So, yes, far, far longer than a month.

inference.note: Duration >1 month rules out F23.3. Persistent persecutory delusions plus clear auditory hallucinations for ~20 months makes F20.0 more likely than F22, but delusional disorder remains a consideration; substance-induced options F15.5 and F12.5 are less likely based on current history but not fully excluded without collateral/toxicology, so narrowed off the active list.

doctor.intent: Determine whether there has been a clear period of prominent mood symptoms, which would argue against delusional disorder and help distinguish schizophrenia from psychotic disorder due to another medical condition.
doctor.question: Have you had a period of at least several days when you felt unusually energetic and needed much less sleep than usual?

target_item.reason: The doctor is asking about manic or hypomanic symptoms (feeling unusually energetic, decreased need for sleep), which are not present in my symptom profile.

patient.answer:
Energetic? Needing less sleep? No... no, doctor, absolutely not. I mean, look at me. I'm sixty-two years old, I've been operating heavy industrial equipment for most of my adult life, and I can tell you right now, there is never a day, let alone a stretch of several days, where I wake up feeling energetic. Honestly, I don't even really remember what that word feels like anymore. If anything, I am just so unbelievably drained. I mean, completely worn down to the absolute nub. 

Now, do I get very little sleep? Yes. Yes, I do, but it's certainly not because I don't need it. I need it desperately. My body aches, my lower back from riding those old suspension seats over the cracked concrete floors all shift... I am exhausted, doctor. Deeply, truly exhausted. But how can a man sleep? How can you close your eyes and drift off when you know the dispatch system is tracking you? When you know that the second you let your guard down, that radio chatter is going to start up again, calling out my operator number, telling everyone I'm a liability. 

So I sit there, awake, but I'm not buzzing with energy or feeling on top of the world or anything like that. I'm just trying to survive the night. I'm just holding on, gripping the steering wheel in my garage, trying to keep my eyes open because I have to stay vigilant. I have to be ready for when security finally comes. But energetic? No. No, I've never had a period like that. I'm just tired. I've been tired for... well, for twenty months, at the very least. It's just a heavy, bone-deep tiredness that never goes away, no matter how much I wish I could just shut the whole network off and sleep for a week. So, no, definitely no bursts of energy. Just exhaustion.

doctor.intent: Determine whether there is a medical or neurologic cause for the psychosis, which would help distinguish a primary psychotic disorder from psychotic disorder due to another medical condition.
doctor.question: Before these experiences began, had you been diagnosed with any brain or nervous system illness, such as a seizure disorder, stroke, Parkinson’s disease, or a head injury?

target_item.reason: The doctor is asking about a history of neurological or medical conditions (like seizures, stroke, Parkinson's, or head injury) to rule out organic causes for the symptoms. This specific medical history is not covered by any item in my symptom profile.

patient.answer:
Brain illness? A stroke, or... Parkinson's? No. No, doctor, nothing like that. I've never had any kind of neurological condition, no seizures, no head injuries... well, I mean, I've bumped my head on the overhead guard of the forklift a few times over the years, sure. Anyone who's driven a Class IV or Class V lift truck for as long as I have knows you're going to take a knock or two when you're rushing to meet a loading quota. But a real injury? A concussion or something that would put me in the hospital? Never. 

I've always been healthy in that regard. My brain has always worked just fine. In fact, it has to. You don't survive in logistics, managing the kind of tonnage I do, if your brain isn't firing on all cylinders. You have to calculate load centers, turning radiuses, weight distribution... all of that requires a sharp mind. If I had Parkinson's, my hands would be shaking, right? I wouldn't be able to operate the hydraulic levers with any precision. I'd be dropping pallets of fragile merchandise all over the loading dock. And if I'd had a stroke, well, they do those DOT physicals, you know? They check your vision, your reflexes, your blood pressure. If there was anything wrong with my nervous system, the company doctor would have flagged my medical card years ago. 

They would have pulled my certification so fast... and like I said, they are looking for any excuse. If I had a medical condition like that, they wouldn't need the dispatch system to build a profile on me, would they? They could just say I'm medically unfit for duty and wash their hands of me. But they can't do that, because my physicals are clean. My brain is fine. It's the system that's the problem, doctor, not my brain. I don't have any of those diseases you just mentioned. I'm just a man trying to do his job while the entire network is actively trying to dismantle my life.

doctor.intent: Determine whether there is a medical cause for the psychosis by checking for a temporal link to prescribed medications such as steroids or dopamine-acting drugs, helping distinguish F06.2 from primary psychotic disorders.
doctor.question: Did these experiences start soon after you began taking any prescribed medication?

target_item.reason: The doctor is asking whether the symptoms were induced by prescribed medication, which is an exclusionary criterion. There is no item in my symptom profile related to medication or substance use.

patient.answer:
Prescription medication? Like... pills from a doctor? No. No, it wasn't anything like that. I mean, I take a little something for my blood pressure, sure—lisinopril, I think it's called. The company doctor put me on it maybe... gosh, maybe five or six years ago? But that's just a tiny little pill I take in the morning with my coffee before I head to the warehouse. It hasn't changed. The dosage hasn't changed, the brand hasn't changed, nothing. I just go to the pharmacy on Main Street, pick up my little bottle every ninety days, and that's it. 

I don't take anything else. No new prescriptions, no painkillers—even though my back is absolutely killing me most days from those suspension seats, I just take over-the-counter ibuprofen. I don't mess with the heavy stuff. You can't operate a ten-ton forklift if you're loopy on prescription painkillers, doctor. OSHA would have a field day with that, and like I keep saying, management is just waiting for me to slip up. If they caught me taking something strong, they wouldn't need the dispatch radio to run me out. They'd just drug test me and fire me on the spot. 

So, no, there were no new medications. Nothing changed in my routine. I was just doing my job, doing the same thing I've done for decades, taking my same blood pressure pill, drinking my same black coffee, driving my same route to work... and then, twenty months ago, the system just... shifted. The scanners started acting up, the error codes started targeting me. It had absolutely nothing to do with anything I swallowed. It was the network. The network changed, doctor, not my medication. I can promise you that. If it was just a pill causing all this, don't you think I would have just stopped taking it? I would have thrown the bottle in the trash a year and a half ago just to get some peace and quiet. But no, it's not a pill. It's the system.

doctor.intent: Determine whether there are prominent negative symptoms, which would help distinguish schizophrenia from delusional disorder or psychotic disorder due to another medical condition.
doctor.question: Have you become less interested in seeing other people or doing things you used to enjoy?

target_item.name: Loss_of_Interest
target_item.manifestation: Fishing, choir practice, and tinkering with wood in the garage used to settle me, but now I can look right at my rods or tools and feel no pull to touch them.
target_item.reason: The doctor is asking about a decrease in interest or pleasure in activities and socializing, which corresponds to the 'Loss_of_Interest' symptom.

patient.answer:
Interested? In... in doing things? Yeah. Yeah, I suppose you could say that. I mean, that's... that's all gone, too. 

I used to have things that settled me, doctor. You know? After a ten-hour shift on the concrete, dealing with the noise and the diesel fumes and the quotas... I had my ways of winding down. Fishing, for one. I used to love getting out by the reservoir, just the quiet of it. Taking my little aluminum boat out, casting a line, not even caring if I caught a single bluegill. It was just about the water. And choir practice—I used to sing bass at the community church down on 4th street. Every Wednesday night for practice, Sunday mornings for the service. It was good to see folks, to harmonize, to feel like you were part of something... normal, I guess. 

And my garage... I've got a whole setup in there. A lathe, a solid oak workbench, clamps, a drill press. I used to spend hours just tinkering with wood in the garage, turning bowls or making little planter boxes. The smell of the sawdust, the feel of the grain under a piece of fine sandpaper... it really used to settle my mind. It gave me peace.

But now? Now... I don't know. It's like someone just reached in and pulled the plug on all of it. 

I sit out in that garage now, like I was telling you, just hiding out in my car, trying to stay awake... and I can look right at my tools. I can look right at my fishing rods leaning up against the drywall in the corner, right next to my tackle box. And there is just... nothing. Absolutely no pull to touch them. I stare at the chisels and the wood glue, and it's like I'm looking at rocks on the moon. They don't mean anything to me anymore. I don't even have the urge to pick them up to dust them off. 

And as for seeing people... the choir director called a few times when I first stopped showing up, asking where I was, if I was sick. I just let it ring. I didn't pick up. I don't want to see them. I don't want to see anybody, really. The thought of standing up there in the robes, trying to smile and make small talk about the weather or the logistics business... it just feels completely impossible. I just don't have the interest. I don't have the spark for any of it. I look at the things I used to love, and it's all just dead weight now.

doctor.intent: Determine whether the psychosis is due to a general medical condition by checking for cognitive decline, which would favor F06.2 over primary psychotic disorders.
doctor.question: Have you noticed your memory getting worse?

target_item.reason: The doctor is asking about memory loss or cognitive decline, which is not covered by any of the items in my symptom profile.

patient.answer:
Memory? Like... forgetting where I put my keys or... or not knowing what day it is? No. No, doctor, nothing like that. If anything, my memory is working overtime right now. It's almost too sharp, to be perfectly honest with you. 

You see, in my line of work, you absolutely cannot afford to have a bad memory. I've got an associate's degree, sure, but out on the warehouse floor, it's all about what you can hold in your head in real-time. We've got hundreds of thousands of square feet of inventory. I know exactly where the heavy-duty automotive parts are stored compared to the fragile electronics. I don't even need to look at the zone map anymore. I know that bay 47 has a slight dip in the concrete that you have to take at an angle so you don't tip a heavy load. I remember the exact weight limits for the different racking systems. You just... you absorb it, and you hold onto it. 

And lately, with everything going on... with the network and the dispatch system... I have to remember every single detail. I don't have a choice. I have to keep track of it all. I remember the exact sequence of the error codes that pop up on my scanner. Like last Thursday, it was error code 4-0-9-Delta, right at 2:14 PM. I didn't even have to write it down, it's just burned into my brain. I remember the license plates of the delivery trucks that idle too long near my specific loading dock. I remember the exact tone of the automated voice on the radio when it reroutes me. I track all of it in my head because I have to know what the system is doing. 

So, no, my memory isn't slipping at all. I know exactly what I did yesterday, and I know exactly what my life was like twenty months ago before all this started. I remember how things used to be. Honestly, sometimes I wish my memory was getting worse. When I'm sitting out in my car in the garage, trying to stay awake, I remember how quiet my life used to be, how peaceful it was out on the reservoir... and it just makes it harder. But no, my brain is holding onto every single piece of information, every single detail, whether I want it to or not. No memory problems here.

doctor.intent: Determine whether there are prominent disorganized speech or thought-process abnormalities, which would help distinguish schizophrenia from delusional disorder or psychotic disorder due to another medical condition.
doctor.question: Has anyone told you that your speech is hard to follow or that your thoughts seem jumbled?

target_item.reason: The doctor is asking about disorganized speech or jumbled thoughts (formal thought disorder), which is not present in my symptom profile.

patient.answer:
Jumbled? No. No, nobody has ever said anything like that to me. Not once. 

If anything, I’m probably the only one making any actual sense down at the warehouse these days. You have to understand, doctor, when you are operating heavy machinery—when you're moving ten thousand pounds of automotive parts on a forklift—you cannot afford to have jumbled thoughts. And you certainly can't have jumbled speech. We use two-way radios to communicate with dispatch and the floor managers. It’s loud in there, you’ve got backup alarms beeping, diesel engines idling, the ventilation fans roaring... so when you key that mic, you have to be crystal clear. 

I use standard protocol. Clear, concise, exact. "Bay 12 is clear, inbound freight is ready for unloading." "Pallet jack needed at zone four." That sort of thing. I’ve never had a trucker tell me they couldn't understand my directions when I'm telling them which dock to back into. I’ve never had management tell me I'm not making sense when I report my daily totals. My thoughts are lined up perfectly straight, just like the inventory on the racks. 

Now, do they actually *listen* to me when I try to explain what the dispatch system is doing? When I try to show them how the network is targeting my specific scanner with those error codes? No. They brush me off. They tell me to just pull the battery out and put it back in, or they tell me to get back to work and stop worrying about the IT department's business. But that is absolutely not because my speech is hard to follow. They hear the words coming out of my mouth perfectly fine. They understand exactly what I'm saying. They just don't want to deal with it, or maybe they're part of why management is waiting for me to slip up, I don't know. 

But my thoughts? My thoughts are sharp. Like I said before, I'm keeping track of every single detail, every code, every time the automated voice reroutes me. You can't do that if your brain is a mess. I can lay out everything that's been happening to me for the last twenty months, step by step, from the moment I clock in at 5:30 AM to the moment I pull out of that employee lot. I lay it all out perfectly straight. So no, doctor, no one has ever accused me of being jumbled. I know exactly what I'm saying.

doctor.intent: Determine whether there has been a sustained decline in work or self-care functioning outside the delusional system, which helps distinguish schizophrenia from delusional disorder and psychotic disorder due to a medical condition.
doctor.question: Aside from avoiding people and hobbies, have you had trouble keeping up with basic daily tasks like bathing, dressing, cooking, or managing things at work?

target_item.name: Functional Impairment
target_item.manifestation: After the forklift incident, I was taken off operating duties and put on leave because they said I was no longer safe around the equipment. At home, my wife has had to take over bills, appointments, and most chores because I cannot keep up with them reliably.
target_item.reason: The doctor is asking about the patient's ability to keep up with daily tasks, chores, and work responsibilities, which directly assesses functional impairment.

patient.answer:
Trouble keeping up... yeah. Yeah, I suppose that’s... that’s the reality of it right now. 

It’s funny you mention managing things at work, because... well, I’m not actually *at* work right now. Not on the floor, anyway. You see, doctor, there was... an incident. With the forklift. I was telling you earlier how I track everything, how I know the warehouse like the back of my hand, but... well, management didn't see things my way. After the incident, they actually pulled me into the front office—the main office with the glass windows overlooking the floor, not just the floor manager's little desk by the loading bays—and they took me off operating duties entirely. They put me on leave. They sat across from me and actually said I was no longer safe around the equipment. Me! After all my years navigating those narrow aisles without so much as clipping a rack. But they said I wasn't managing the floor safely anymore, so... they put me on leave. 

And at home... well, it’s not much better there, to be perfectly honest with you. My wife... she’s an absolute saint, she really is, but she has had to take over basically everything. I used to handle all our finances. I had a system, I kept track of the mortgage, the water bill, the insurance premiums... I used to balance the checkbook every Sunday evening. But lately? I just... I can't keep up with any of it reliably. I look at a stack of mail on the kitchen counter and it just feels like a mountain I can't climb. I can't process it. So she does it all now. 

She pays the bills, she handles the bank accounts. She even has to manage my schedule—she’s the one who set up this appointment, actually, and she's the one who keeps track of when I'm supposed to be where, because I just can't keep it straight in my head to care about it. And the chores around the house... I used to mow the lawn every Saturday morning, edge the driveway, take care of the gutters in the fall. Now, I just sit out in the car in the garage. She's doing the cooking, the laundry, taking the trash bins down to the curb on Tuesday nights. I just... I can't seem to manage any of those basic things anymore. It’s like all my energy is just tied up in trying to stay awake and figure out what the system is doing, so she just... she has to do everything for me.

doctor.intent: Differentiate a primary psychotic disorder from a psychotic disorder due to a medical condition by checking for visual hallucinations, which would raise suspicion for an organic cause in this older patient.
doctor.question: Have you seen things that other people could not see?

target_item.name: Hallucinations
target_item.manifestation: Even when I'm sitting in my garage with everything shut off, I hear dispatch voices clear as day calling my operator number and saying I'm dangerous or that security is coming for me.
target_item.reason: The doctor is asking about visual hallucinations, which falls under the general symptom category of hallucinations.

patient.answer:
See things? Like... like visions or shadows or something? No, no. My eyes work perfectly fine. I have to get my vision checked every single year to keep my operator certification current, 20/20 with my bifocals. I don't see anything that isn't physically right there in front of me on the concrete. 

But... well, hearing things... that's a different situation entirely. That's what's really been keeping me on edge. 

I mentioned earlier that I spend a lot of time sitting out in my car in the garage these days. My wife, she probably thinks I'm just out there trying to get some peace and quiet, maybe listening to the sports radio or something. But I don't even have the key in the ignition. The engine is off. The garage door is pulled all the way down and locked. It's supposed to be dead silent in there. We live at the end of a cul-de-sac, doctor, so there isn't even any street traffic to make a sound. 

But even then... even when I'm sitting in my garage with absolutely everything shut off... I hear them. I hear the dispatch voices. And it's not just a faint mumble through the walls, it is clear as day. It sounds exactly like the two-way radio is still clipped right there on my high-vis vest. I hear that little static click when someone keys the mic, and then I hear them calling my exact operator number. Four-two-seven-niner. They call my number, and they talk about me on the open channel. They say that I'm dangerous. They actually use that exact word, 'dangerous,' like I'm some kind of threat to the facility after all my years of clean safety records! 

And then... then they say that security is coming for me. I'll just be sitting there in the dark, gripping the steering wheel of my sedan, and I hear dispatch telling the floor managers that security is en route to apprehend me. I know I'm at home, I know I'm on leave and not on the clock, but I hear it so clearly

doctor.intent: Determine whether there is a prominent mood syndrome occurring alongside the psychosis, which would argue against delusional disorder and help separate schizophrenia from an organic psychotic disorder.
doctor.question: During these last twenty months, have you felt depressed most of the day nearly every day?

target_item.name: Additional Requirement 2
target_item.manifestation: For most of this whole trouble, even when the warehouse fears were quieter for a bit, I was still down, empty, and unable to get myself back into fishing, woodworking, or family meals.
target_item.reason: The doctor is asking if the depressive symptoms have been present for the majority of the time over the last twenty months, which directly assesses if the depressive episode is present for the majority of the total duration of the illness.

patient.answer:
Yeah... twenty months. It’s hard to even wrap my head around it being that long, but... yes. Yes, I have. Most of the day, nearly every single day, just like you said. It’s like dragging a ten-ton pallet of lead weights around with me everywhere I go. 

You know, the thing is, there were times during all of this trouble—stretches where those warehouse fears I was telling you about, the dispatch voices and the panic about security—there were times when all of that actually quieted down for a little bit. Where my mind wasn't racing quite so fast about the automated system and I wasn't sitting in the car gripping the steering wheel quite so tight. But even then... even when that part of it gave me a bit of a breather... I was still just so incredibly down. Just... empty. Completely hollowed out inside, like someone had just pulled the plug and drained everything out of me. 

I used to be such an active guy on my weekends. I’ve got a beautiful bass boat sitting under a tarp next to the driveway, and I haven't even checked the battery on it in over a year. I have a full woodworking setup in the back half of the garage—table saw, drill press, a really nice lathe my wife got me for my fiftieth birthday. I used to spend hours out there turning these custom oak bowls, making things with my hands. But I just... I couldn't get myself back into any of it. Not the fishing, not the woodworking. Even when the warehouse stuff wasn't front and center, I couldn't even bring myself to sit down for family meals anymore. My wife would make a whole Sunday roast, set the dining room table, and I just couldn't sit there with them. I just felt too empty to participate in my own life. So, yes, doctor, it's been a constant heavy cloud this whole time, no matter what else was going on.

inference.note: Added F25.1 because patient reports a pervasive major depressive syndrome for most of the 20-month illness, and psychotic symptoms have at times persisted even when the warehouse-related fears/voices were quieter, raising schizoaffective disorder vs schizophrenia. F22 remains less likely because persistent auditory hallucinations and functional decline are more than typical for delusional disorder. F06.2 still not excluded by history alone, though no neurologic/medication/substance trigger identified.

doctor.intent: Determine whether there was at least a two-week period of hallucinations or delusions occurring without any depressive symptoms, to distinguish schizoaffective disorder from schizophrenia.
doctor.question: Was there ever a period of at least two weeks when you were hearing the dispatch voices or believed the warehouse system was targeting you, but you were not feeling depressed?

target_item.name: Additional Requirement 3
target_item.manifestation: There was a stretch when my mood had eased some and I was eating and talking a little more, but for several weeks I still heard dispatch calling my number and believed the routing system was tracking me.
target_item.reason: The doctor is asking if there was a period of at least two weeks where the patient experienced psychotic symptoms (hearing voices, believing the system was targeting them) without feeling depressed, which directly corresponds to Additional Requirement 3 (Criterion B for Schizoaffective Disorder).

patient.answer:
Well, you know, it’s funny you ask that specific question, because... yes. Yes, actually, there was a time like that. It’s hard to keep the timeline perfectly straight sometimes with everything going on, but I remember this one period clearly because it was just so... strange. 

There was a stretch—it lasted for several weeks, actually—when that heavy cloud, that ten-ton pallet of lead weights I was telling you about, it actually lifted for a bit. My mood had eased some. I wasn't feeling that crushing emptiness every single minute of the day. I was actually coming out of the garage, coming back into the house, and sitting down at the dining room table again. My wife had made her pot roast, the one with the little red potatoes and the thick gravy, and I actually ate a full plate. I was eating, and I was talking a little more, too. Just about normal things, you know? The weather, the neighbor's dog, the price of gas. It felt... well, it felt like I could finally take a breath. 

But the thing is, doctor... the warehouse never left me alone. Not even then. 

Even during those several weeks when I was feeling better, when I wasn't depressed and I was eating and talking with my wife... I still heard them. I'd be sitting right there at the dinner table, chewing my food, and I would hear the static click. I still heard dispatch calling my number. Four-two-seven-niner. Clear as a bell, right in my ear, talking about how dangerous I was. And on top of that, I still believed the routing system was tracking me. You know the automated routing system we use for the pallets? The one that scans the barcodes and directs the forklifts through the aisles? I knew, without a shadow of a doubt, that it was tracking my movements right there in my own house. 

It’s just... it's so hard to explain to someone who hasn't lived it. How can you feel alright, you know, relatively speaking—how can your mood be fine, but you're still completely convinced that an industrial warehouse computer is mapping your kitchen? But that's exactly what was happening for those weeks. I'd just sit there, having a totally normal conversation with my wife, passing the salt, all while knowing the routing system had locked onto my coordinates and dispatch was monitoring my every move. So, yes, the mood got better for a few weeks, but the rest of it... the rest of it didn't stop at all.

inference.note: Psychosis has persisted for >2 weeks during a period when he was not depressed, which rules against psychotic depression and supports schizoaffective disorder, depressive type. Long duration with auditory hallucinations, persecutory delusions, functional decline, and negative symptoms also keeps schizophrenia in the differential. Delusional disorder is ruled out by prominent hallucinations and marked impairment; organic psychosis is less supported by lack of neurological/medication/substance cause.

opening_question.intent: Understand the patient's main reason for seeking psychiatric care today
opening_question.question: Hi, it’s good to meet you. What brings you in today?

final_diagnosis.reason: The patient has persistent psychotic symptoms for about 20 months, including persecutory delusions and auditory hallucinations, with functional decline. In addition, he reports a sustained depressive syndrome present most days over the same period, with anhedonia, social withdrawal, low energy, and impaired daily functioning. Crucially, he also describes several weeks of ongoing hallucinations/delusions when he was not depressed, supporting schizoaffective disorder, depressive type, over schizophrenia. There is no evidence of manic episodes, substance-induced etiology, medication cause, or neurological disorder.
